docs.title: Known LLM API hostnames
docs.text:
The proxy only intercepts CONNECT requests to these hostnames (everything else is tunnelled raw, no MITM):

  • api.openai.com
  • api.anthropic.com
  • generativelanguage.googleapis.com
  • cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com (Gemini CLI OAuth)
  • bedrock-runtime.*.amazonaws.com
  • *.openai.azure.com
  • api.mistral.ai
  • api.groq.com
  • api.together.xyz
  • api.deepseek.com

Extend at runtime with:

tracker.register_provider(
    name="openrouter",
    base_url="https://openrouter.ai",
    path_patterns=("/api/v1/chat/completions",),
)

This updates two places at once: the shared ProviderRegistry (subprocess intercept hosts — addons see new hosts via shared reference), and the in-process httpx-patch path set (so _is_llm_request returns true for the new path).

docs.title: Why each piece exists
docs.text:
Every layer of complexity is forced by a real constraint, not a design choice:

  1. We want to observe LLM calls → patch httpx in-process
  2. But subprocess agents have their own httpx → need a network proxy
  3. But network traffic is encrypted → need MITM with fake certificates
  4. But the agent rejects fake certificates → need a custom CA in the trust store
  5. But we need to know which calls belong to which combo → use a separate port per session
  6. But os.environ isn't safe for parallel subprocesses → pass env explicitly to each subprocess instead of mutating globals
  7. But state dies with the Python process and other languages can't share it → run the same proxy code as a long-lived agentopt serve daemon; clients pick local vs daemon via the AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL env var, with no API change

docs.title: Scoping constraints
docs.text:
1. Python only — the proxy is Python. CA trust config targets Python and Node HTTP clients (SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS).
  2. HTTP only — no gRPC, no WebSocket. HTTP/HTTPS covers 99%+ of current LLM API traffic.
  3. mitmproxy for CONNECT/TLS — pinned mitmproxy>=12,<13. The from-scratch HTTP CONNECT handler we used to maintain (~1100 lines of socket / ssl / http.client) is gone; mitmproxy handles framing, TLS termination, HTTP/2, and certificate generation correctly by construction.
  4. One DumpMaster per session — keeps the lifecycle simple and avoids depending on mitmproxy's undocumented runtime mode-update behavior. Tradeoff: ~100-300ms startup and ~30MB RSS per concurrent session.
  5. Docker uses sidecar proxy — the proxy runs inside the container. Self-contained, no host networking dependency.

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
The one non-obvious correctness invariant we still own:

  • Token-usage extraction must not silently report zero. A successful (HTTP 200) call whose usage we can't parse is a real proxy gap, not a 0-token call. usage.py raises UsageExtractionError with a diagnostic naming exactly which keys it searched and which were present; Recorder attaches that to CallRecord.error and uses a <parse-failed> sentinel for the model name so the failure surfaces in result summaries.
  • Late records must not be dropped. A blocking upstream request can finish after the session's track() scope exits. SessionManager.add_record looks up both active and ended sessions so the late record lands in the archive instead of being lost.

(The previous CONNECT-prelude-buffering and strict-Content-Length invariants are now mitmproxy's problem, not ours.)

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. CA certificate compatibility: do any Python LLM SDKs override SSL_CERT_FILE or pin certificates? Need to test against openai, anthropic, google-generativeai, boto3.

  2. Agents that bypass HTTPS_PROXY: some SDK versions may hardcode direct connections. Mitigation: maintain a compatibility matrix per SDK version.

  3. Real-time streaming forwarding: SSE / Transfer-Encoding: chunked responses are parsed correctly today (the SSE token-extractor handles Anthropic's split message_start / message_delta usage events and Gemini's usageMetadata), but the proxy currently buffers the full upstream response before sending it back to the client — so the client doesn't see chunks land in real time. For evaluation workflows this is fine (you read the final result anyway). For interactive use you'd want chunk-by-chunk forwarding while still accumulating SSE frames for token extraction.

docs.title: SelectionResults
docs.text:
Returned by selector.select_best(). Holds every evaluated combination and the metadata needed to inspect, export, and compare them.

Method Returns Description print_summary() None Print a ranked table with accuracy, latency, tokens, and price. When any result has combined_objective set, the table sorts by that value. get_best(attribute=None) ModelResult? The is_best combination. Pass attribute to scope the lookup to a single metric track. get_best_combo() Dict[str, str]? Best combination as {"node": "model_name"}. get_by_attribute(attribute) List[ModelResult] All results for a given attribute. to_csv(path) None Export every result to CSV. export_config(path, api_key_env_vars=None) None Export the best combination as a LiteLLM-style YAML config; api_key_env_vars overrides per-provider env-var names.

Iterable: for result in results: ... yields ModelResults.

Top-level fields are available on both live snapshots and the final result:

Field Meaning results Observed configuration results, including partial evaluations where the method supports them. is_final False for progress snapshots; True for the final callback and returned result. stop_recommended Stopping advice from single-objective Gittins; False for other methods. It is independent of whether the run has ended. stop_reason Current phase or final stopping reason. A user-requested stop reports user_stopped; adaptive methods report search_cost_budget at a dollar cap; UCB reports evaluation_failed when an entire acquisition batch produces no observation. total_evaluations Successful configuration–question evaluations represented in the results. Failed evaluations may incur selection_cost without increasing this count. selection_wall_time_seconds Elapsed selection time at the snapshot. selection_cost New non-cached search spending in USD; None when pricing is unavailable. search_cost_overshoot_usd Actual spending above the optional soft dollar cap for Gittins, UCB, and Bayesian optimization; zero without a cap.

Pass on_update to select_best() to receive independent snapshots. selector.latest_results returns a copy of the latest snapshot, or None before the first update. Observations can appear before a recommendation is eligible: Gittins needs a complete warm start, and random selection needs a complete configuration or shared-question sweep. A current recommendation can change as more data arrives. See live selection for stopping and update boundaries.

docs.title: GittinsSelectionResults
docs.text:
Gittins returns a SelectionResults subclass with these additional fields:

Field or method Meaning objective_mode "single" or "multi". recommendations / get_recommendations() Recommended configurations at the snapshot, with predicted accuracy/cost, standard deviations, conservative coordinates, node-to-model combo, and observed sample count. Single mode defaults to zero uncertainty penalty; multi mode defaults to one standard deviation. stop_reason Final reasons include user_stopped, question_budget, search_cost_budget, warm_start_budget, all_arms_completed, gittins_stop (single with automatic stopping enabled), and direction_eta_numerical_floor (multi). Live snapshots can report warming_up or running. stop_recommended Single-objective Gittins' model-based advice to stop. Advice can change with subsequent observations. Advice alone does not end the run: the default stop_on_recommendation=False continues evaluating. Check is_final and stop_reason for actual termination. total_evaluations Successful configuration–question evaluations, including warm start. search_cost_overshoot_usd Actual non-cached spend above the optional soft dollar cap. direction_eta Current multiplier of each search direction. Single mode reports [1.0]; its separate cost_scaling_factor stays fixed. choose(max_cost_usd=..., min_score=..., cost_weight=...) Select a candidate using conservative deployment criteria; returns a recommendation or None if infeasible.

ModelResult.accuracy, price, and combined_objective describe observed data. Recommendation accuracy and cost_usd predict the supplied dataset's full mean; objective and conservative_objective describe the scalar prediction in single mode. The two kinds of values must not be conflated. Single mode marks one is_best when a candidate is eligible. Multi mode marks none: use the recommendation set and a deployment preference instead. See Gittins for assumptions, budget guards, and Gaussian uncertainty semantics.

docs.title: RandomSelectionResults
docs.text: Random baselines expose the same recommendation and choose(...) interface, plus sampling and completed_units. Their score/cost values are empirical means from complete configurations or shared-question sweeps. Conservative fields equal the means; zero std fields mean no uncertainty model was fitted. Partial units are retained in evaluation records but excluded from recommendations. In single mode, get_best() and get_best_combo() identify an eligible empirical winner; in multi mode, use get_recommendations() and choose(...). Both random methods report actual search cost, but do not accept a dollar cap or issue stopping advice.

docs.title: Single-objective example
docs.text:
results = selector.select_best(parallel=True)
results.print_summary()

best = results.get_best()
if best is not None:
    print(f"Best: {best.model_name}, accuracy={best.accuracy:.1%}, ${best.price:.6f}/sample")

results.to_csv("all_results.csv")
if best is not None:
    results.export_config("optimized_config.yaml")

docs.title: ModelResult
docs.text:
One per evaluated combination.

Field Type Description model_name str Combination label, e.g. "planner=gpt-4o + solver=gpt-4o-mini". accuracy float Mean eval score across evaluated datapoints. combined_objective float? Mean per-datapoint combined score when lambda_cost and/or lambda_latency were set on the selector; None otherwise. See selectors.md — Combined objective. latency_seconds float Mean latency per datapoint. input_tokens Dict[str, int] Input tokens by model. output_tokens Dict[str, int] Output tokens by model. attribute str Metric track the result was scored under. is_best bool Whether this is the top-ranked combination. datapoint_results List[DatapointResult] Per-datapoint breakdown.

Properties:

Property Returns total_input_tokens int Sum across models. total_output_tokens int Sum across models. price float? Per-sample USD cost, or None if pricing for any used model is unavailable. num_samples int len(datapoint_results), with 1 as the fallback for failed combos.

str(result) returns a one-line "name (accuracy: X%, latency: Ys, tokens: {…}, price: $…)" summary.

docs.title: DatapointResult
docs.text:
Per-datapoint detail inside ModelResult.datapoint_results.

Field Type Description datapoint_index int Index in the dataset. score float Eval score. latency_seconds float Latency for this datapoint. input_tokens Dict[str, int] Input tokens by model. output_tokens Dict[str, int] Output tokens by model.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
A Router is a policy that decides — per individual LLM call — which model to send the request to. The swap happens transparently at the HTTP layer, so it works with any framework (OpenAI SDK, Anthropic, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI) and any subprocess agent (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, etc.) — no integration code.

from agentopt import LLMTracker, RandomRouter

router = RandomRouter(candidates=["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini"], seed=0)
with LLMTracker(router=router) as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):  # session per datapoint
            agent.run(q)                       # each LLM call routed independently
tracker.print_summary()                        # model sequence, tokens per model, total latency

router= on LLMTracker alone sets a default that nested tracker.track() calls inherit; the per-datapoint sessions give the summary something to group by. If you don't need per-datapoint attribution, drop the inner with and pass a combo_id= to LLMTracker instead — the tracker will open one session for the whole block.

The same code works whether the proxy runs in-process (default) or through a long-lived agentopt serve daemon (AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL=… env var) — setting the env var is the entire deployment switch.

docs.title: Why routing (vs. selection)
docs.text:
A model selector picks one combination of models and evaluates it on the whole dataset. A router is orthogonal: given a pool of candidate models, it decides at runtime, for every LLM call, which one to use — based on the prompt, session metadata, or prior calls in the same workflow.

ModelSelector Router Grain One combo per experiment One model per call Decision time Before the run At each HTTP request Natural algorithm Gittins, random, UCB, Bayesian Rule-based, classifier, bandit Activation selector.select_best() with LLMTracker(router=...)

docs.title: Public API
docs.text:
from agentopt import Router, RandomRouter, LLMTracker

RouteContext (the type of ctx on Router.route) lives at agentopt.routing.RouteContext — only needed if you want a type annotation; most custom routers just access fields by attribute.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
Member Description route(ctx) -> Optional[str] Implement this. Return a model name to swap, or None to keep the client's choice. config() / _config_kwargs() Wire serialization for daemon mode. Override _config_kwargs() to enable custom routers to travel to the daemon.

The Router class itself is not a context manager — activate it by passing it to LLMTracker(router=...) (or tracker.track(router=...)). The tracker owns the session and the records.

docs.title: RouteContext
docs.text:
Read-only by contract — request_body is wrapped in types.MappingProxyType, so ctx.request_body["foo"] = bar raises TypeError. (Shallow guarantee: nested lists/dicts like messages stay mutable. Don't mutate them — cache keys and recording read the same dict.)

Field Type Description request_body Mapping[str, Any] Parsed inbound JSON (read-only view). provider str "openai", "anthropic", "google", or "unknown". requested_model str? The model the client originally asked for. session SessionInfo Active session (data_id, combo_id, agent_id, records). history Sequence[CallRecord] Snapshot of prior calls in this session.

docs.title: RandomRouter
docs.text:
RandomRouter(candidates: Sequence[str], seed: int | None = None)

Uniform random pick. seed makes choices reproducible.

docs.title: LLMTracker (relevant surface for routing)
docs.text:
Member Description LLMTracker(combo_id=..., router=...) Single-session sugar: __enter__ opens a tracking session with the given IDs and router; __exit__ closes it. Pass router= alone (no ID) and it's a default for nested track() calls instead. tracker.track(data_id=..., combo_id=..., router=...) Multi-session host pattern. Inherits the constructor's router= when not overridden. tracker.records All CallRecords captured by this tracker. tracker.print_summary(data_id=..., combo_id=...) Model sequence, per-model tokens, total latency. Grouped by data_id when records span multiple distinct values.

See tracker.md for the full tracker surface (cache, providers, queries, lifecycle).

docs.title: Writing a custom policy
docs.text:
Subclass Router and implement route:

from agentopt import LLMTracker, Router

class FirstCallBigRouter(Router):
    """Big model on the first call of a workflow, cheap model after."""

    def __init__(self, big: str, small: str) -> None:
        self.big = big
        self.small = small

    def route(self, ctx):
        return self.big if not ctx.history else self.small

router = FirstCallBigRouter(big="gpt-4o", small="gpt-4o-mini")
with LLMTracker(router=router) as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):
            agent.run(q)
tracker.print_summary()
  • Return None to keep the requested model.
  • Exceptions inside route() are caught and logged; the request proceeds unrouted. A router must never break an agent.
  • One policy per file, mirroring agentopt.model_selection — drop new policies into agentopt/routing/ as siblings of random_policy.py.

docs.title: Daemon mode
docs.text: When AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL is set, the same Python code routes via the daemon — Router.config() serializes the router and POSTs it on POST /sessions; the daemon reconstructs it from a registry and applies it in its mitmproxy addon.

docs.title: Default policy at startup
docs.text:
Configure a daemon-wide default that applies to every session that doesn't carry its own:

agentopt serve --routing-policy random \
    --candidate-models gpt-4o,gpt-4o-mini \
    --seed 42

Currently only random is wired to CLI flags. Pass --candidate-models without --routing-policy and the daemon refuses to start.

A client running against this daemon simply opens sessions — no router code, no router import:

with LLMTracker() as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):
            agent.run(q)
tracker.print_summary()

docs.title: Per-session override
docs.text:
To override the daemon's default for one session, pass router= to the client's LLMTracker (or to tracker.track()):

router = RandomRouter(candidates=["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini"], seed=0)
with LLMTracker(router=router) as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):
            agent.run(q)

The override applies only to sessions opened by this tracker — other clients on the same daemon keep using the default. To run a session unrouted against a daemon that has a default, drop down to the wire protocol (see proxy.md for POST /sessions's router field).

docs.title: Custom routers in daemon mode
docs.text:
Custom Router subclasses work over the wire too. The daemon just needs to import the module the class lives in. Two ways:

  1. --policy-module path/to/my_policies.py — daemon pre-imports the file at startup; classes inside resolve as "<file-stem>:ClassName". Repeatable.
  2. PYTHONPATH — put the module on the daemon process's sys.path (start the daemon from a CWD that contains it, or set PYTHONPATH). importlib.import_module does the rest.

docs.title: What --policy-module expects
docs.text:
A plain Python file. No plugin manifest, no register() callback, no decorators. Three rules:

  1. Define Router subclasses at module level so getattr(module, "ClassName") finds them.
  2. Each class must implement _config_kwargs() if you want clients to push it per-session — returns a JSON-serializable dict of __init__ kwargs. (Daemon-default policies set from the CLI don't need this, but per-session overrides from Python clients do.)
  3. __init__ must accept that dict back as kwargs. The daemon reconstructs the router with cls(**kwargs).

That's the whole contract.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
# my_policies.py
from agentopt import Router


class FirstCallBigRouter(Router):
    """Big model on the first call of a workflow, cheap after."""

    def __init__(self, big: str, small: str):
        self.big = big
        self.small = small

    def route(self, ctx):
        return self.big if not ctx.history else self.small

    def _config_kwargs(self):
        return {"big": self.big, "small": self.small}

agentopt serve --policy-module ./my_policies.py

Client side (Python with AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL set):

from agentopt import LLMTracker
from my_policies import FirstCallBigRouter      # import for client-side use

router = FirstCallBigRouter(big="gpt-4o", small="gpt-4o-mini")
with LLMTracker(router=router) as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):
            agent.run(q)
tracker.print_summary()

Under the hood, LLMTracker calls router.config() → {"policy": "my_policies:FirstCallBigRouter", "kwargs": {"big": "...", "small": "..."}} → POSTs to the daemon → daemon resolves via importlib.import_module("my_policies") (already in sys.modules from --policy-module) → instantiates.

docs.title: What you DON'T need to add
docs.text:
• No POLICIES = {...} dict
  • No register(registry) function
  • No __main__ block
  • No entry-point declaration in pyproject.toml (though you can package it that way if you'd rather pip install it than point at a file)

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• The file stem becomes the module name. routes.py → routes:MyRouter. Avoid stdlib collisions (random.py, json.py, logging.py) — your file would shadow the stdlib module inside the daemon process.
  • Module-level code runs at daemon startup. Imports and class definitions are fine; heavy work (tokenizers, classifiers) is fine but blocks startup. If your module raises, the daemon won't start.
  • Repeat the flag for multiple files: --policy-module ./a.py --policy-module ./b.py.
  • No hot reload. Restart the daemon to pick up edits.
  • Class identity matters only at wire-decode time. What goes over the wire is (policy_string, kwargs_dict). The Python client's class needs to produce a policy_string whose module:Class resolves on the daemon to the right class — the simplest way is for client and daemon to import the same file (PYTHONPATH or shared installable package).

Security: the daemon imports whatever file you point it at, so don't --policy-module from untrusted sources. v1 is localhost-only — anyone who can POST to the daemon already has local execution, so this matches the existing trust model.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The swap happens at the same HTTP-layer seams the proxy already uses for tracking and caching:

  • In-process httpx path — LocalHandler in agentopt.proxy.interceptor. The patched httpx.Client.send dispatches to the active session's handler, which applies the router and rebuilds the request with the new body["model"] (a fresh httpx.Request so its .stream and Content-Length stay coherent).
  • Subprocess path — AgentoptAddon.request in agentopt.proxy.mitm_addon. The mitmproxy addon owned by the session reads the same router and mutates flow.request.content.

Both sites delegate to one shared dispatcher in agentopt.routing.base.apply_router:

agent.run(q)
  └── httpx.Client.send  →  patched send  →  active.handler.handle_sync
      └── apply_router(router, body, path, session)
          └── ctx = RouteContext(body, provider, requested_model, session, history)
          └── model_name = router.route(ctx)
          └── body["model"] = model_name  (if not None)
      └── (post-routing) cache lookup, forward to upstream, record

Cache keys reflect the routed model, not the requested one. Routing runs before _make_cache_key, so two identical request bodies routed to different models produce distinct cache entries. Otherwise a routed call could return a response generated by a different model.

docs.title: v1 limits
docs.text:
• Same-provider only. route() returns Optional[str] — a model name in the same provider as the request URL. Cross-provider routing (host + auth + schema rewrites) is on the roadmap.
  • OpenAI / Anthropic body shape only. The model lives in request_body["model"]. Gemini's URL-encoded model (/v1beta/models/{model}:generateContent) isn't rewritten yet — route() is still called, but a non-None decision logs at DEBUG and the request passes unrouted.
  • Custom routers in daemon mode require an importable module — either --policy-module ./file.py or PYTHONPATH. Routers must also implement _config_kwargs() so they serialize over the wire (the base class raises a clear error otherwise).

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text:
src/agentopt/routing/
├── base.py            Router, RouteContext, apply_router dispatcher, config/_config_kwargs
├── random_policy.py   RandomRouter
├── config.py          BUILTIN_POLICIES registry + resolve_policy()
├── summary.py         print_routing_summary, format_routing_summary
└── __init__.py        public re-exports

Top-level re-exports: agentopt.Router, agentopt.RandomRouter.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
• Gemini path-rewrite routing — extend the dispatcher to rewrite /v1beta/models/{model}:… URLs when the body has no model field.
  • Cross-provider routing — route() -> Optional[str | RouteDecision]; RouteDecision carries provider/api_key and the dispatcher rewrites host + auth + (where required) the request schema. Streaming response translation is the hard part.
  • Selection ↔ routing loop — feed ModelSelector results into a learned Router (bandit, classifier on prompt features) so selection and routing compound rather than merely coexist. ModelSelector doesn't accept a router= parameter yet.

docs.title: Selectors
docs.text:
ModelSelector evaluates combinations of models for an agent against a supplied dataset. method="auto" uses Gittins. objective_mode="single" returns one configuration; objective_mode="multi" returns an accuracy–cost recommendation set.

from agentopt import ModelSelector

selector = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent, models=models, eval_fn=eval_fn, dataset=dataset,
    method="auto", objective_mode="single", cost_scaling_factor=1e-4,
    max_search_cost_usd=10.0,
)
results = selector.select_best(parallel=True, max_concurrent=4)
print(results.get_best_combo())

docs.title: Common parameters
docs.text: Parameter Meaning agent Class accepting a model dictionary in __init__ and implementing run(input_data). models Node names mapped to nonempty candidate lists. dataset Nonempty sequence of (input_data, expected_answer) pairs. eval_fn (expected, actual) -> float, higher is better. Gittins and random selectors validate against score_bounds. method Algorithm name; default "auto" uses Gittins. objective_mode "single" (default) or "multi". Invalid method/mode combinations fail before tracking starts. model_prices Custom prices in USD per million tokens: {"model": {"input_price": x, "output_price": y}}. tracker Optional LLMTracker; otherwise one is created. Tracking starts in the constructor and stops when select_best() returns or raises. lambda_cost, lambda_latency Optional deployment penalties for single mode, both default 0.0. See below.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
method Single Multi auto, gittins Gittins finite-dataset winner CC-Gittins two-axis recommendation set random Random complete configurations — ucb UCB-E over configuration–question observations — bayesian Categorical GP with Log Expected Improvement — random_configurations Random complete configurations Random complete configurations random_questions Shared random questions across all configurations Shared random questions across all configurations

random is the single-mode alias for random_configurations. matrix_ucb is an alias for ucb. Bayesian optimization requires the optional agentopt-py[bayesian] dependencies; the other methods are available in the standard installation.

docs.title: Live recommendations and user stopping
docs.text:
Every supported method accepts select_best(on_update=None, stop_event=None) in addition to parallel and max_concurrent. on_update(snapshot) receives an independent result snapshot after completed work and once more with is_final=True when selection finishes. Inspect total_evaluations, selection_cost, selection_wall_time_seconds, and the current recommendation to update a display. In multi mode, display get_recommendations() instead of a single winner.

from threading import Event

stop = Event()

def update_display(snapshot):
    print(f"Evaluations: {snapshot.total_evaluations}")
    print(f"Search cost: {snapshot.selection_cost}")
    if snapshot.get_best_combo() is not None:
        print(f"Current recommendation: {snapshot.get_best_combo()}")
    if snapshot.is_final:
        print(f"Stopped: {snapshot.stop_reason}")

results = selector.select_best(
    parallel=True, max_concurrent=4,
    on_update=update_display, stop_event=stop,
)

A UI action or another thread can call stop.set() or selector.request_stop(). A callback can request a stop by returning False; returning None continues selection. selector.latest_results returns a copy of the most recently published snapshot, or None before the first update. The callback runs in the selection thread, so keep it brief and follow your UI framework's rules for updating widgets from a worker thread.

Stopping is cooperative: the currently scheduled batch finishes, including work queued behind the concurrency limit. Its observations and costs are recorded, and no following batch is scheduled. The final reason is user_stopped. A stop request does not cancel an LLM request or refund its cost. Progress and stopping checks occur at these boundaries:

Method Update boundary Recommendation readiness Gittins Each warm-start evaluation, then each adaptive batch No recommendation until the uniform warm start finishes; subsequent recommendations use finite-dataset predictions. Random configurations Each sequential evaluation or concurrent chunk of questions Only complete configurations are eligible. Random questions Each configuration evaluation within a shared-question sweep Only complete sweeps contribute to recommendations. UCB Each acquisition batch Ranks observed configurations by their current empirical scalar means; these are partial-data estimates without calibrated uncertainty. Bayesian optimization Each complete configuration, or completed parallel acquisition batch Ranks fully evaluated configurations.

A snapshot can contain observations but no eligible recommendation. Further evaluations may change a recommendation in either direction; the displayed score is not a guarantee of improvement or future performance.

Budgets are optional, and every run has a finite dataset. Use a fraction to choose the evaluation allowance in advance, a user stop to decide while watching results, or both. Gittins, UCB, and Bayesian optimization also accept an optional soft dollar cap. Random baselines report spending without using a dollar cap.

docs.title: Evaluation fractions and budgets
docs.text:
Let K be the number of configurations and N the number of dataset questions. A configuration–question cell is one agent evaluation; the full grid has K × N cells. A cell fraction is not a fraction of distinct dataset questions: adaptive methods can allocate different questions to each configuration.

Method Fraction parameter and default How the allowance is spent max_search_cost_usd Gittins observation_budget_fraction=1.0 of K × N cells Uniform warm start, then adaptive batches Optional soft cap, with estimates before adaptive batches Random configurations observation_budget_fraction=1.0 of K × N cells Whole configurations, N cells each Unsupported; spending is reported Random questions observation_budget_fraction=1.0 of K × N cells Shared-question sweeps, K cells each Unsupported; spending is reported UCB observation_budget_fraction=1.0 of K × N cells Adaptive cell batches Optional soft cap, checked between acquisition batches Bayesian optimization sample_fraction=0.25 of K configurations Complete configurations; at least two when available Optional soft cap, checked between configurations or parallel acquisition batches

Cell fractions are rounded up to a whole cell. Random baselines start only complete units that fit, so a remainder can be unused: a 0.5 fraction means approximately half the configurations for random_configurations, or half the questions shared across all configurations for random_questions. Gittins and random also accept max_total_question_evaluations as an absolute cell cap. Gittins' cap must fund its warm start; random's must fund one complete unit.

Single-objective Gittins additionally publishes stop_recommended. Advice does not end the run by default: stop_on_recommendation=False keeps selecting unfinished configurations until a user stop, a budget, or full completion. Set it to True to end automatically with stop_reason="gittins_stop". Multi-objective Gittins retains its own direction/eta termination rule. The advice can change as further observations arrive. A recommendation to stop, user_stopped, and budget exhaustion are separate signals; inspect is_final and stop_reason to tell whether a run has ended.

docs.title: Combined objective (optional cost/latency weights)
docs.text:
Single mode optimizes the evaluation score by default. To express a scalar deployment preference:

objective = score - lambda_cost × norm(cost) - lambda_latency × norm(latency)

Gittins fixes its min/max scales from warm-start observations; subsequent values can lie outside those initial ranges. Random selection uses common min/max scales from completed sampling units. UCB and Bayesian optimization use running min/max scales across observed samples and refresh the stored scalar objectives. A constant or unavailable scale contributes zero; a positive cost weight requires known prices.

These deployment weights are separate from Gittins' search-cost coefficient cost_scaling_factor. The latter defaults to 1e-4 in single mode and multiplies raw USD evaluation costs inside the DP. It does not change the final deployment score. Multi mode rejects nonzero deployment lambda weights; use results.choose(...) instead.

docs.title: Gittins: single and multi objective
docs.text:
Each configuration receives a seeded independent permutation of question indices and a uniform warm start. The live tracker supplies token attribution and pricing. Every evaluation must have tracked token usage and all recorded calls must have known nonnegative prices; supply model_prices for custom models. Evaluation or pricing failures abort selection and stop tracking.

parallel=True runs questions within the selected adaptive batch concurrently, up to max_concurrent. Warm-start questions run sequentially so a dollar cap can be checked after each evaluation. Async agents work in both modes.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning objective_mode "single" One scalar winner or a two-objective recommendation set. batch_size 4 Questions evaluated per adaptive visit. warm_start_batch_size 4 Questions per configuration before adaptation, clamped to dataset size. observation_budget_fraction 1.0 Maximum fraction of configuration–question cells, including warm start. max_total_question_evaluations None Absolute cell limit, combined with the fraction cap. max_search_cost_usd None Soft cap on new non-cached token charges, including warm start. cost_scaling_factor 1e-4 Single only: fixed search penalty per USD of expected evaluation cost. prior_mean 0.5 Single only: fixed prior mean in normalized score units (also used for the optional scalar objective). recommendation_beta None Resolves to 0.0 in single mode and 1.0 in multi mode. recommendation_min_samples 0 Minimum observed questions for recommendation eligibility. score_bounds (0.0, 1.0) Finite permitted score range; normalized affinely for inference. prior_variance 0.04 Normalized accuracy/scalar prior variance. score_noise_variance 0.25 Per-question accuracy noise variance. Weighted single mode scales scalar noise with the deployment weights. cost_reference_usd None Multi cost-axis scale, inferred from the largest warm configuration mean; one USD if all warm costs are zero. search_cost_scale_eta 1.0 Multi only: scale applied to workflow-cost continuation penalties. eta_initial, eta_decay 1.0, 0.5 Multi only: initial per-direction eta and decay on a direction stop. effective_cost_bin_ratio 2.0 Multi only: cost binning for DP reuse; None disables it. effective_cost_bin_anchor 1e-4 Multi only: USD anchor for cost bins. grid_size 129 DP interpolation resolution, at least 17. stop_tolerance 1e-9 Numerical stopping comparison tolerance. stop_on_recommendation False Single only: end automatically when Gittins recommends stopping; otherwise publish the advice and continue. seed 42 Nonnegative seed for question permutations.

docs.title: Single-objective index and stopping
docs.text:
Single mode uses the posterior mean of the complete finite dataset for acquisition, stopping, and recommendation. With N questions, n observed values with sum S, and a Gaussian latent posterior (m, v):

finite mean = (S + (N - n) × m) / N
finite variance = ((N - n)² × v + (N - n) × question_noise) / N²

The DP has one transition per question, even when the next selected configuration is evaluated in a batch. The finite-mean transition variance is the latent-mean transition variance multiplied by a², where a = 1 + question_noise / (N × prior_variance). Costs retain their monetary scale:

DP cost per question = cost_scaling_factor × warm mean question cost in USD

Costs and lambda remain fixed after warm start. A tiny positive numerical floor (1e-12) handles zero or extremely small DP costs. The cost coefficient has units of normalized score per USD; changing cost units requires changing this coefficient. The default 1e-4 does not guarantee a particular evaluation budget.

A completed configuration's index is its exact empirical scalar mean. When the best completed value reaches the largest unfinished index, single mode publishes stop_recommended=True. This is a model-based assessment of whether more evaluation is worth its cost. The default stop_on_recommendation=False continues with the highest-index unfinished configuration; it does not reduce the search-cost coefficient. Set stop_on_recommendation=True to end on the advice with stop_reason="gittins_stop". User stopping, cell/dollar budgets, and full completion can also end a run.

The winner maximizes finite_mean - recommendation_beta × finite_std, with lower conservative deployment cost breaking ties. At the default beta of zero this is posterior-mean recommendation. Warm-start calibration of unknown live costs is an adaptation to online evaluation; configurations with known fixed costs can have different trajectories in an offline replay.

docs.title: Multi-objective search and recommendations
docs.text:
Multi mode follows the CC-Gittins deployment and quality axes in 1:1 round-robin order. Both directions share all observations. Warm observations determine the Gaussian plug-in calibration and expected continuation costs, which remain fixed. When a direction stops, its eta decreases; the run ends when both directions stop at numerical eta floors without an intervening observation, or when a budget/full completion ends it.

Recommendations are the strict non-dominated set of (accuracy_mean - beta × accuracy_std, cost_mean + beta × cost_std) over eligible configurations, using finite-dataset moments. Two search axes do not limit the output to two configurations. Multi mode does not set a unique is_best: get_best() and get_best_combo() return None, and export_config() cannot export a unique best configuration.

results = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent, models=models, eval_fn=eval_fn, dataset=dataset,
    objective_mode="multi", max_search_cost_usd=10.0,
).select_best()
for candidate in results.get_recommendations():
    print(candidate.combo, candidate.conservative_accuracy, candidate.conservative_cost_usd)
chosen = results.choose(max_cost_usd=0.01)  # highest score within cost limit
# Also supported: choose(min_score=0.85), choose(cost_weight=20.0)
if chosen is not None:
    print(chosen.combo)

choose(cost_weight=w) maximizes conservative score minus w × raw_USD. Infeasible preferences return None. The returned recommendation does not change is_best. Model-based estimates describe the supplied finite dataset; they do not guarantee joint coverage, performance on future questions, or the complete true frontier. The two-axis protocol and offline reproductions are described in AgentOpt Research.

docs.title: Budget accounting
docs.text:
The cell cap must fund the uniform warm start. A dollar cap reached during warm start returns observed records, stop_reason="warm_start_budget", and no recommendations. Search spending excludes cache hits; deployment costs include their recorded workflow usage.

Before adaptive evaluation, Gittins checks the planned batch's frozen estimate of new charges. Actual charges can exceed that estimate; the result reports the excess as search_cost_overshoot_usd. Unused budget can remain when the next complete adaptive batch does not fit. A user-supplied cell cap is enforced without overshoot.

docs.title: Random baselines
docs.text:
random_configurations selects configurations without replacement and evaluates each on every question. random_questions selects questions without replacement and evaluates each on every configuration. Both support single and multi mode; random is the single-mode configuration-sampling alias. Single mode recommends the highest empirical scalar mean among eligible configurations; multi mode returns their empirical accuracy–cost frontier. No all-configuration warm start or Gaussian model is used.

No budget argument is required: by default, both methods evaluate the finite configuration–question grid unless the user stops them. Both accept observation_budget_fraction=1.0, max_total_question_evaluations=None, seed=42, and score_bounds=(0, 1). The fraction refers to K × N cells. The cap must fund a whole configuration (N cells) or shared-question sweep (K cells), and each new unit must fit the remaining cell cap. Thus an unused cell remainder is possible.

Random baselines do not accept max_search_cost_usd. They allocate an evaluation allowance independently of measured cost and report actual non-cached search spending in selection_cost. Configuration sampling can evaluate its questions concurrently. A user stop can interrupt a unit; its observations remain in evaluation records but are excluded from recommendations. For shared questions, only fully completed sweeps enter single-mode rankings or the multi-mode empirical frontier. This gives every eligible configuration the same observed questions.

RandomSelectionResults supports get_recommendations() and choose(...) and adds sampling and completed_units. Recommendation score/cost are empirical means on complete units. Conservative fields equal these means; zero standard-deviation fields indicate no uncertainty model, not certainty about unseen data.

docs.title: UCB and Bayesian optimization
docs.text:
UCB (ucb, alias matrix_ucb) uses mean + sqrt(a/n), with a=1.0, and samples unseen questions on the selected configuration. observation_budget_fraction=1.0 caps cells; sample_fraction is an alias that takes precedence. seed controls question sampling. max_concurrent controls both the batch size and concurrency, and parallel is ignored. If an entire acquisition batch fails to yield an observation, UCB stops with stop_reason="evaluation_failed".

Bayesian optimization uses a categorical MixedSingleTaskGP and Log Expected Improvement. Each selected configuration is evaluated over the complete dataset. If some questions fail, successful observations remain in the results, but that configuration is excluded from GP training and recommendations. sample_fraction=0.25 caps the number of configurations (at least two if available); batch_size=1 controls configurations per GP iteration. Both baselines support scalar deployment weights, single-objective recommendations, evaluation fractions, anytime user stopping, and max_search_cost_usd=None.

Their dollar cap counts new non-cached token charges, including evaluation and judge calls. Costs must be known when a cap is requested. The cap is checked before scheduling further work: UCB can exceed it by the current acquisition batch; Bayesian optimization can exceed it by the current complete configuration, or by all configurations in the current parallel acquisition batch. Smaller batches reduce the work between spending checks. These are soft spending limits, not guarantees of an exact dollar total.

docs.title: agentopt.model_selection.gittins.GittinsModelSelector
docs.text:
Gittins with scalar or two-axis accuracy/cost objectives.

Included in the standard installation (NumPy and SciPy). No complete score matrix is needed. Each combination receives a seeded independent question order and a uniform warm start; no cell is evaluated twice in one run.

single optimizes score, optionally penalizing cost and latency with fixed warm-start min/max scales. multi keeps score and mean USD as separate objectives; scalar lambda weights are invalid in that mode.

observation_budget_fraction counts cells including warm start. max_search_cost_usd counts actual non-cached token charges including warm start. Before adaptive batches, their frozen warm-start charge estimates are reserved. Actual costs may exceed estimates, so this is a soft spend cap; any overshoot is reported. A cap interrupting warm start returns observed records and an empty recommendation set.

Single mode prices each question with cost_scaling_factor=1e-4 times its estimated USD cost. It uses a fixed prior (prior_mean=0.5 in normalized units), finite-dataset means and per-cell DP transitions. Its default recommendation_beta is zero; multi mode defaults to one. Single mode recommends stopping when a completed empirical value reaches every unfinished index, keeping the cost coefficient fixed. By default it continues selecting the largest unfinished index until a budget, user stop, or full completion. Set stop_on_recommendation=True to stop automatically.

In multi mode, a direction stops when a completed arm's value reaches the maximum unfinished Gittins index. Its eta then decays; all directions must stop at numerical floors without an intervening observation to halt globally. Budget exhaustion and full completion can halt earlier. Evaluation or pricing failures abort the run, with the base selector stopping tracking.

docs.title: agentopt.model_selection.random_search.RandomSearchModelSelector
docs.text:
Randomly evaluate complete configurations or shared questions.

Configuration sampling evaluates every question for each chosen random configuration. Question sampling evaluates every configuration on each chosen shared random question. Both sample without replacement.

Evaluation caps fund whole units. Users can stop at any time; an interrupted partial unit is excluded from empirical recommendations. All evaluations require tracked, priced token usage to report search spending and deployment costs.

docs.title: agentopt.model_selection.matrix_ucb.MatrixUCBModelSelector
docs.text:
UCB on the full combination × datapoint matrix (row means + exploration bonus).

Selection always proceeds in batches of matrix cells; only select_best(..., max_concurrent=...) matters (parallel is ignored).

observation_budget_fraction or, equivalently, sample_fraction (same meaning as in Bayesian optimization: fraction of the search budget — here, fraction of matrix cells to observe) caps evaluations. 1.0 fills the full grid; 0.1 stops after about 10% of cells. If both are passed, sample_fraction wins.

max_search_cost_usd optionally stops scheduling batches once observed search spending reaches the cap. The last scheduled batch may exceed it.

docs.title: agentopt.model_selection.bayesian_optimization.BayesianOptimizationModelSelector
docs.text:
Select models via Bayesian optimization.

max_search_cost_usd optionally caps observed search spending. Each configuration is evaluated in full; a scheduled configuration or parallel acquisition batch finishes before the cap is checked again.

docs.title: Tracker
docs.text:
LLMTracker is the single primitive that captures LLM calls — by token usage, latency, model, and request/response — across every agent shape AgentOpt supports (in-process SDKs, subprocess CLIs, container agents). Selection and routing both build on it; you can also use it standalone for tracking and caching.

from agentopt import LLMTracker

The same code runs against the in-process proxy (default) or a long-lived gateway daemon (AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL=…). The env var is the entire deployment switch — no API change.

docs.title: Plain tracking (no router, no selector)
docs.text:
with LLMTracker(combo_id="run-1") as tracker:
    agent.run(prompt)
print(tracker.get_usage())

docs.title: Per-datapoint sessions
docs.text:
with LLMTracker() as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):
            agent.run(q)
tracker.print_summary()         # grouped by data_id

docs.title: With a router
docs.text:
from agentopt import LLMTracker, RandomRouter

router = RandomRouter(candidates=["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini"], seed=0)
with LLMTracker(router=router) as tracker:
    for i, q in enumerate(questions, 1):
        with tracker.track(data_id=f"q{i}"):
            agent.run(q)
tracker.print_summary()

router= alone is not single-session sugar — it sets a default that nested tracker.track() calls inherit, so the host pattern above works.

docs.title: Subprocess agent
docs.text:
While a track() scope is active, LLMTracker patches subprocess.Popen so every child spawned inside it inherits HTTPS_PROXY + the merged CA bundle path automatically — no env-var plumbing in the agent's run():

import subprocess

with LLMTracker(combo_id="subproc") as tracker:
    subprocess.run(["claude", "-p", prompt])

Merge policy — explicit beats implicit:

  • env=None (caller said nothing — inherit os.environ): {**os.environ, **session_env}. Session wins over any HTTPS_PROXY the parent shell happened to set.
  • env=<dict> (caller wrote an explicit env): {**session_env, **user_env}. Caller's keys win on conflicts. Setting e.g. env={"HTTPS_PROXY": "http://custom-proxy:8080"} inside a track() scope is respected — agentopt never silently overrides an explicit env. The common case env={"PATH": ...} (set for non-LLM reasons) still gets tracking because the user didn't write the session keys, so session_env fills them in.

Limitations of the ContextVar-based activation (same as the httpx patch):

  • A new threading.Thread doesn't propagate _active_session_var automatically — subprocess calls inside the thread won't be intercepted. Workaround: wrap the thread target with contextvars.copy_context().run(...).
  • multiprocessing.Process (spawn mode) starts a fresh Python interpreter that never called tracker.start(), so the patch isn't installed there. Fork mode inherits the patch and works.

For agents that ignore HTTPS_PROXY and instead need the proxy URL / CA cert injected into a config file (OpenClaw is the canonical case), agentopt.get_current_session_proxy() is the escape hatch — see the helper below. See proxy.md for the full subprocess flow.

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
LLMTracker(
    *,
    data_id: str | None = None,
    combo_id: str | None = None,
    agent_id: str | None = None,
    router: Router | None = None,
    cache: bool = True,
    cache_dir: str | Path | None = ".agentopt_cache",
)
Param Description data_id / combo_id / agent_id If any is set, __enter__ auto-opens a single tracking session with those IDs and __exit__ closes it. The "single-session sugar" path. router A Router to apply at the proxy layer. On its own it sets a default that nested track() calls inherit; combined with one of the IDs above it also routes the auto-opened session. cache Enable response caching. Hits short-circuit before any network round-trip. cache_dir Persist cache to disk at this path. Pass None to keep it in memory only.

AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL is read in __init__; when set, the tracker delegates to RemoteBackend and cache_dir is honored by the daemon, not the client.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
Method Description start() Install the httpx redirect and prepare the backend. Idempotent. stop() Tear down live sessions, restore httpx, flush cache. Record queries remain valid after stop() — so tracker.print_summary() works right after a with block exits. close() Final teardown. For RemoteBackend this drops the long-lived control-plane HTTP client; for LocalBackend it's equivalent to stop(). Idempotent.

__exit__ calls stop(), not close() — so post-with queries against the daemon don't fail with "client closed". Call tracker.close() explicitly when you want to release the HTTP client (or let __del__ do it).

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
@contextmanager
tracker.track(
    data_id: str | None = None,
    combo_id: str | None = None,
    agent_id: str | None = None,
    router: Router | None = None,
) -> SessionInfo

Open a tracking session. In local mode this eagerly spins up a per-session mitmproxy SessionMaster on an ephemeral port and sets a ContextVar so in-process httpx calls are attributed correctly. In daemon mode it POSTs /sessions and reuses the daemon's port.

All four params are optional. router= falls back to the router passed to LLMTracker(...) if you don't supply one here.

Helper Description get_session_env(session) {HTTPS_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS} for subprocess agents. Identical shape in both modes. agentopt.get_current_session_proxy() Module-level convenience — reads the active session from the ContextVar and returns a SessionProxy (url, port, ca_pem, ca_bundle_path, env_dict()). Returns None outside a track() scope.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text: Method Returns Description records (property) List[CallRecord] All records captured so far. get_records(data_id=None, combo_id=None, agent_id=None) List[CallRecord] Filtered records. get_usage(...) Dict[str, Tuple[int, int]] {model: (input_tokens, output_tokens)} aggregated over matching records. get_cached_latency(...) float Total latency (seconds) of cache-hit records — useful for "how much wall time did caching save?" print_summary(data_id=None, combo_id=None, agent_id=None) None Model sequence, per-model tokens, and total latency. Grouped by data_id when records span multiple distinct values; flat otherwise. Thin wrapper over agentopt.routing.print_routing_summary.

docs.title: Cache & providers
docs.text:
Method Description flush_cache() Flush dirty cache entries to disk. clear_cache() Drop all cached responses (memory + disk). clear() Clear locally archived records. register_provider(name, base_url, path_patterns) Add or replace an LLM provider so its hostnames are MITM-intercepted and its paths recognized by the in-process patch. In daemon mode this also POSTs /providers to keep the daemon in sync.

Cache keys hash the routed model (not the requested one), so a router swapping gpt-4o → gpt-4o-mini produces a distinct cache entry. See router.md.

docs.title: CallRecord
docs.text:
from agentopt import CallRecord
Field Type Description data_id str? Datapoint identifier. combo_id str? Model-combination identifier. agent_id str? Agent role identifier. model str Model name (the one actually used after any routing). prompt_tokens int Input tokens. completion_tokens int Output tokens. latency_seconds float API call duration. request_url str Upstream URL. request_body dict Parsed request payload. response_body dict Parsed response payload. timestamp str ISO 8601. cached bool Whether this was a cache hit. error str? Set when the upstream failed or token extraction couldn't parse a successful response. The model name is "<parse-failed>" in the latter case so the failure surfaces in summaries.

docs.title: Use with ModelSelector
docs.text:
ModelSelector instances accept a tracker= kwarg. By default they construct one internally and call start() in the constructor / stop() when select_best() returns. Pass your own when you want to share a cache across runs, point at a daemon, or post-process the records after selection completes:

tracker = LLMTracker(cache_dir="./shared_cache")
selector = ModelSelector(agent=..., models=..., tracker=tracker, ...)
results = selector.select_best()
# tracker has been stopped, but records remain queryable:
print(tracker.get_usage())

See selectors.md for the full constructor surface.

docs.title: ResponseCache (low-level)
docs.text:
from agentopt.proxy import ResponseCache

Usually owned by LLMTracker. Exposed for tests and advanced setups:

Method Description get(key) Look up a cached entry. put(key, entry) Store an entry (dirty until flush). flush() Write dirty entries to SQLite. clear() Drop memory + disk. close() Flush and stop the background flush thread.

docs.title: Why Your Agent Needs a Model Combo Optimizer, Not Just a Model
docs.text:
Wenyue Hua*, Qian Xie, Sripad Karne, Armaan Agrawal, Nikos Pagonas, Kostis Kaffes, Tianyi Peng*

* Equal contribution

Most teams pick a model, usually the latest frontier release, and run every step of their agent on it. Planner? GPT-5.4. Solver? GPT-5.4. Critic? GPT-5.4. It works, so nobody questions it.

But "it works" is not "it's optimal." What if the same accuracy costs 20x less with a different combination? What if a weaker model actually performs better at one of those steps? These aren't hypotheticals. We ran the experiments.

docs.title: Server-Side vs User-Side: Who's Optimizing What?
docs.text:
There's a lot of exciting work happening in LLM inference optimization. Systems like Autellix, ThunderAgent, and Continuum tackle it from the provider's side: batching requests, quantizing weights, routing traffic across GPU clusters, speculatively decoding tokens. This is server-side optimization. It makes the provider more efficient, and some of those savings trickle down to you through lower prices.

But there's a completely different optimization surface that these systems don't touch: which models you choose to run in the first place.

Server-side optimization saves the provider's money. User-side optimization saves your money. And the gap between the best and worst model choice is far larger than anything server-side tricks can close.

docs.title: What User-Side Optimization Actually Means
docs.text:
Every LLM-powered agent lives in a three-axis tradeoff space:

  • Quality: does it get the right answer?
  • Cost: how much do you pay per query?
  • Latency: how long does the user wait?

You can't maximize all three. A frontier model like Claude Opus gives you the best quality but costs more and runs slower. A small model like Ministral 3 8B is cheap and fast but less capable. The question is: where on this tradeoff surface do you want to be?

No server-side system can answer that for you. Only you know your quality requirements, your budget, and your latency SLA. A startup building a coding assistant might happily trade 5% accuracy for 10x cost savings. A medical AI can't afford to trade accuracy at all.

This is why the user must own the objective function. AgentOpt lets you define exactly what "good" means for your use case through a simple eval_fn, and then finds the model combination that optimizes for it.

docs.title: Model Selection Is the Foundation of Everything Else
docs.text:
Among all the optimization levers available to you (caching, routing, speculative decoding, request scheduling), model selection is the one that dominates. Not because the others don't matter, but because model selection is upstream of all of them.

Think about it: if you don't know which model to run, what do you cache? Which GPU do you route to? What workload profile do you schedule for?

Caching, routing, and scheduling all assume you've already decided which model to use. They're optimizations applied on top of a model choice. Model selection is the prerequisite they all depend on.

And the impact is enormous. Here's what we found across three benchmarks, comparing the most expensive combination to the cheapest one that achieves similar accuracy:

Benchmark Expensive Combo Acc Cost Budget Combo Acc Cost Savings GPQA Opus 74.75% $2.47 gpt-oss-120b 68.18% $0.19 13x HotpotQA Opus + Opus ~32% $2.02 Qwen3 Next + gpt-oss-120b 71.8% $0.13 16x MathQA Opus + Haiku 4.5 98.8% $6.19 gpt-oss-20b + Kimi 94.6% $0.26 24x BFCL Opus 70% $60.13 Qwen3 Next 70% $1.90 32x

These are real numbers from real benchmarks. Same accuracy band, 13-32x cost difference. No amount of caching or request batching can close a 32x gap. The model choice is the optimization.

docs.title: Agent Routing Is Not LLM Routing
docs.text:
If you've seen LLM routing systems (the ones that pick GPT-5.4 for hard questions and GPT-4o for easy ones), you might think: "Can't I just do that for each step of my agent?"

No. And here's why.

In single-request LLM routing, credit assignment is trivial. One call, one output, one score. You can directly measure which model is better for which type of query.

In a multi-step agent, the steps interact. The planner's output shapes what the solver sees. A critic's feedback loops back to the generator. There's no intermediate ground truth: you can only score the final output. Was the answer wrong because the planner gave bad instructions, or because the solver couldn't follow good ones? You can't tell by looking at each step in isolation.

This makes credit assignment non-trivial. You can't decompose "pick the best model per layer" into independent decisions. The layers affect each other.

The principled response is to treat the combination as the atomic unit. Don't optimize layers independently. Evaluate full combos end-to-end.

And the results prove why this matters. On HotpotQA (multi-hop question answering with a planner + solver architecture), we found something that no per-layer optimization would ever discover:

The weakest planner + the strongest solver beats the strongest planner + any solver.

Ministral 3 8B (the cheapest, smallest model) as planner paired with Claude Opus as solver achieves 74.3% accuracy. Claude Opus as both planner and solver? Only ~32%. Why? Because Opus as planner is too capable: it answers the question directly, bypassing the solver's search tools entirely. The "worse" planner correctly delegates to the tool-augmented solver, producing better results.

You'd never find this by picking "the best model" for each layer independently. The best combo doesn't contain the best individual models. This is the credit assignment problem in action.

docs.title: Reducing the Overhead: Bandits and Bayesian Optimization
docs.text:
There's an obvious objection: if you have to evaluate full combinations, doesn't the search space explode? With M models and N layers, you have M^N combinations. 9 models across 2 layers = 81 combos. Each evaluated on 200 datapoints = 16,200 LLM calls. That's expensive.

This is where search algorithms matter. And a good search algorithm is non-trivial.

docs.title: Arm Elimination
docs.text:
Borrow an idea from multi-armed bandits: treat each model combination as a slot machine arm. You want to find the arm with the highest payout (accuracy) without pulling every arm thousands of times.

The insight: most combinations are clearly bad after just a few samples. You don't need to run all 200 datapoints to know that a combo scoring 40% after 20 samples isn't going to beat one scoring 75%.

Arm Elimination works in rounds:

  1. Start small: evaluate all combos on a small initial batch (e.g., 10 datapoints)
  2. Eliminate: use confidence intervals to statistically identify dominated combos. If a combo's upper confidence bound is below another's lower bound, it's out.
  3. Grow the batch: double the datapoints, evaluate only the survivors
  4. Repeat: until one combo remains or you run out of data

Bad combos get eliminated early and cheaply. Good combos earn more search budget. The search cost is far less than brute force.

docs.title: Bayesian Optimization
docs.text: For expensive evaluations, Bayesian Optimization builds a Gaussian Process surrogate model that predicts accuracy as a function of the model combination. It uses Expected Improvement to pick the most informative next evaluation, spending budget where uncertainty is highest and potential is greatest.

docs.title: How Much Do These Save?
docs.text:
Across our four benchmarks, Arm Elimination consistently achieves near-optimal accuracy while using up to 67% less budget than brute force:

Benchmark Brute Force Accuracy Arm Elimination Accuracy Search cost savings HotpotQA 74.27% 73.19% 67% MathQA 98.84% 98.83% 58% GPQA 74.75% 74.10% 24% BFCL 70.00% 69.37% 12%

Nearly identical accuracy to exhaustive search, at roughly half the search cost. These algorithms don't just save budget. They find the right combo with statistical guarantees.

docs.title: Empirical Validation
docs.text: We validated AgentOpt across four diverse benchmarks using 9 models on Amazon Bedrock:

docs.title: The Benchmarks
docs.text:
• HotpotQA: multi-hop question answering (2-tuple: planner + solver with search tools)
  • GPQA Diamond: graduate-level science questions (1-tuple: single model)
  • MathQA: mathematical reasoning (2-tuple: answer model + critic)
  • BFCL v3: multi-turn function calling (1-tuple: single model)

Format: obtained accuracy / search cost savings vs brute force. Averaged over 50 seeds. Green = within 5% of brute force accuracy AND >50% savings on that metric.

Arm Elimination consistently achieves near-optimal accuracy while using significantly less budget than brute force across our four benchmarks. No single selector dominates all benchmarks — Arm Elimination performs best when there is clear separation between the best combo and the rest (HotpotQA, MathQA), while Bayesian Optimization can achieve high savings on large search spaces at the cost of lower find rates.

docs.title: Selection Algorithms
docs.text:
Choose the output you need with objective_mode, then choose how to allocate evaluations with method. method="auto" uses Gittins in both modes.

Method Objective mode Evaluation strategy Recommendation auto / gittins single Cost-aware Gittins index for the finite dataset's mean score Highest posterior mean score, with an optional uncertainty penalty random / random_configurations single Random configurations, each evaluated on all questions Highest observed mean score among completed configurations random_questions single Shared randomly ordered questions, evaluated on every configuration Highest observed mean score on completed shared-question sweeps ucb single UCB-E: mean score plus sqrt(a / n); random unseen questions on the selected configuration Highest observed mean score bayesian single Categorical Gaussian process and Log Expected Improvement; complete configuration evaluations Highest observed mean score auto / gittins multi CC-Gittins alternating deployment and quality axes Conservative accuracy–cost recommendation set random_configurations multi Random configurations, each evaluated on all questions Empirical accuracy–cost frontier among completed configurations random_questions multi Shared randomly ordered questions, evaluated on every configuration Empirical accuracy–cost frontier on the shared observed questions

All random sampling is without replacement. Multi-objective selection does not designate a unique best configuration. Use results.get_recommendations() to inspect the set and results.choose(...) to express a deployment preference.

docs.title: Gittins
docs.text:
Gittins starts with a small uniform batch to estimate live evaluation costs. Single mode uses a fixed Gaussian prior and the posterior of the complete finite dataset's average score for sampling, stopping, and recommendation. Observed scores contribute directly; the posterior predicts unseen scores. A fully evaluated configuration has its exact empirical score and zero prediction uncertainty.

Each single-objective DP step represents one question. The numerical evaluation penalty is:

DP evaluation cost = cost_scaling_factor × expected question cost in USD

cost_scaling_factor defaults to 1e-4. A larger value favors an earlier stopping recommendation. It stays fixed during a single-objective run. When the best completed configuration is at least as valuable as every unfinished Gittins index, the result reports stop_recommended=True. By default, selection continues with the highest-index unfinished configuration until a user stop, a budget, or full completion. Set stop_on_recommendation=True to end automatically on that advice. The default configuration recommendation maximizes posterior mean (recommendation_beta=0); a positive beta subtracts a multiple of the predictive standard deviation.

The single-objective finite-dataset convention follows BanditGittinsEval. Live uniform warm-up and estimated monetary costs are package adaptations; they are not identical to experiments with known per-arm costs. The coefficient multiplies the supplied cost units: 1e-4 per USD is not numerically equivalent to 1e-4 per unit evaluation or per cost ratio.

Multi mode preserves score and deployment cost as separate objectives. It alternates a deployment-cost axis and a quality axis, shares every observation between the axes, and reduces each direction's eta when that direction stops. Its default recommendations use score mean minus one standard deviation and cost mean plus one standard deviation. These model-based coordinates concern the supplied dataset, not guaranteed future performance or recovery of the complete true frontier.

docs.title: Search cost and deployment preferences
docs.text:
cost_scaling_factor prices search evaluations in single-objective Gittins. max_search_cost_usd is a separate soft cap on new non-cached token charges. Neither parameter subtracts deployment cost from a configuration's score.

For a scalar deployment tradeoff, single-objective selectors accept lambda_cost and lambda_latency (both default to zero). For several tradeoffs, use multi mode and choose from its recommendations using a deployment cost limit, score floor, or cost weight. See the selector reference for the normalization rules and budget semantics.

docs.title: Live recommendations
docs.text:
All methods can publish results through select_best(on_update=...) while the search runs. A user can stop through a shared stop_event, selector.request_stop(), or a callback that returns False. The selector finishes the currently scheduled batch, including queued evaluations, and returns its latest result without scheduling a following batch. Both random methods support this interface in single and multi mode.

The recommendation reflects the evidence available at each update. Random configuration sampling ranks completed configurations; random question sampling uses completed shared-question sweeps. UCB ranks empirical estimates from its partial observations. Bayesian optimization ranks configurations evaluated on the full dataset. Gittins begins recommending after its uniform warm start and uses finite-dataset posterior predictions. Thus an early stop can return observations with no recommendation, and later observations can change a winner.

docs.title: Evaluation allowances and spending
docs.text:
Every method supports an evaluation fraction and anytime user stopping. With K configurations and N questions, observation_budget_fraction for Gittins, UCB, and random means a fraction of K × N configuration–question evaluations. It does not generally mean that only that fraction of distinct questions will be used.

  • Random configurations spend N evaluations per selected configuration, so the fraction approximately specifies a fraction of configurations.
  • Random questions spend K evaluations per shared question, so the fraction approximately specifies a fraction of questions.
  • Gittins and UCB allocate their cell allowance adaptively. Gittins includes its uniform warm start in that allowance.
  • Bayesian optimization's sample_fraction counts configurations, each evaluated on the complete dataset, with a minimum of two configurations when available. It requires pip install "agentopt-py[bayesian]".

The cell allowance is rounded up; random methods require whole units to fit and can leave a remainder. The default evaluation allowance for random, UCB, and Gittins is the complete grid; Bayesian optimization uses sample_fraction=0.25.

Random baselines report spending and offer evaluation limits, without a dollar budget parameter. Gittins, UCB, and Bayesian optimization additionally accept max_search_cost_usd, a soft cap on new non-cached charges. Gittins checks frozen cost estimates before adaptive batches. UCB and Bayesian optimization check actual spending before scheduling their next batch or complete configuration. Work already scheduled can exceed the cap. A budget, a user's stop request, and Gittins' model-based stopping advice express different reasons to end or reconsider a search.

Gittins, UCB, and random baselines are included in the standard installation. See advanced_algorithms.py for runnable examples.

docs.title: Response Caching
docs.text: AgentOpt caches LLM responses at the HTTP level to avoid redundant API calls during model selection.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[LLM Call] --> B{In cache?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Return cached response]
    B -->|No| D[Call API]
    D --> E[Store in memory]
    E --> F[Background flush to SQLite]
Property Detail Cache key SHA-256 of the request path and body (model + messages + params), excluding stream In-memory Thread-safe dict — always active when caching is on On disk Optional SQLite database (cache.db), flushed every 10 seconds by a background thread

Cached responses retain their original token usage and latency measurement. Selection results use these to estimate deployment cost and latency, while selection_cost excludes cache hits because they incur no new provider charge.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
During model selection, many LLM calls are identical:

Shared model calls

If two configurations produce the same planner request, the second can reuse the first response once it is cached. Matching depends on the request path and body, including the model, messages, and parameters. Concurrent cache misses can still make separate provider calls.

Re-running a benchmark

A new run can reuse matching requests from an earlier run, including when only the scoring function changes. New requests or changed prompts can incur charges; scoring and selection still take time.

Stopping and restarting

A user stop ends the selection run after the currently scheduled work completes. AgentOpt does not save or resume a selection checkpoint. Create a new selector to run again, using the same cache directory to reuse saved responses. Cache entries already flushed to disk survive process restarts; an abrupt exit can lose more recent entries.

docs.title: Choosing a Cache Directory
docs.text:
In local mode, LLMTracker() enables caching in .agentopt_cache by default. Set cache_dir to use a benchmark-specific directory:

from agentopt.proxy import LLMTracker

tracker = LLMTracker(cache_dir="./llm_cache")
selector = ModelSelector(
    ...,
    tracker=tracker,
)
results = selector.select_best()
# Cache automatically flushed to ./llm_cache/cache.db

On subsequent runs with the same cache_dir, entries are loaded from disk at startup. Use LLMTracker(cache_dir=None) for memory-only caching. If AGENTOPT_GATEWAY_URL selects daemon mode, cache storage is managed by the daemon rather than these local tracker settings.

docs.title: Cache Lifecycle
docs.text: Event What Happens LLMTracker(cache_dir=...) Creates DB if needed, loads existing entries into memory LLM call (cache miss) Response stored in memory, marked dirty Background flush (every 10s) Dirty entries written to SQLite tracker.stop() / select_best() returns Final flush to disk tracker.clear_cache() Clears memory and deletes all DB rows

docs.title: Disabling Cache
docs.text: tracker = LLMTracker(cache=False)

docs.title: Inspecting the Cache
docs.text:
The cache is a standard SQLite database:

Count entriesInspect stored latencyDatabase size 
sqlite3 ./llm_cache/cache.db "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cache"

sqlite3 ./llm_cache/cache.db "SELECT key, json_extract(data_json, '$.latency_seconds') FROM cache LIMIT 10"

docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph "Your Code (unchanged)"
        A[Agent] --> B[LLM Framework]
    end
    subgraph "Transport Layer"
        B --> C["httpx.Client.send()"]
    end
    subgraph "AgentOpt (transparent)"
        C --> D[Interceptor]
        D --> E[Response Cache]
