    C --> I[LLM API]

docs.title: The Interception Layer
docs.text:
Every major LLM SDK uses httpx for HTTP requests. AgentOpt patches httpx.Client.send() and httpx.AsyncClient.send() at the class level, intercepting every LLM API call transparently:

your_agent(input)
  +-- framework internals (LangChain, CrewAI, etc.)
        +-- httpx.Client.send()   <-- intercepted here
              +-- LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)

This means:

  • Zero code changes to your agent or framework
  • No proxy server to configure
  • Works with any framework that uses httpx (OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, AG2, ...)

Supported providers

Any LLM provider whose SDK uses httpx is automatically supported. This includes OpenAI, Anthropic, Google (Gemini), Mistral, Cohere, and any OpenAI-compatible API endpoint.

docs.title: What Gets Tracked
docs.text:
For each intercepted call, AgentOpt records:

Field Description model Model name (e.g., gpt-4o) prompt_tokens Input token count completion_tokens Output token count latency_seconds Wall-clock API call duration data_id Which datapoint triggered this call combo_id Which model combination was being evaluated cached Whether the response was served from cache

docs.title: Attribution with ContextVars
docs.text:
AgentOpt uses Python's contextvars to attribute LLM calls to the correct datapoint and model combination. Each thread and async task gets its own context, so parallel evaluations never interfere:

with tracker.track(data_id="dp_1", combo_id="gpt4o+haiku"):
    result = agent(input_data)
    # All LLM calls in this block are tagged with dp_1 + gpt4o+haiku

This is what makes parallel=True safe — concurrent evaluations are fully isolated.

docs.title: Response Caching
docs.text:
AgentOpt caches at the HTTP level:

Property Detail Cache key SHA-256 of request body (model + messages + params), excluding stream In-memory Thread-safe dict, always active On disk Optional SQLite database, flushed by background thread

When the same prompt hits the same model, the cached response is returned instantly — preserving the original latency measurement for fair comparisons.

Cache savings in practice

If two model combinations share the same planner model, the planner call for each datapoint is identical and hits the cache. With 9 combinations and 3 planner models, you only pay for 3 unique planner calls per datapoint — not 9.

docs.title: The Selection Loop
docs.text:
For each model combination:

  1. Build — Instantiate the agent class with the candidate models via agent(models)
  2. Run — Execute the agent on every datapoint in the evaluation dataset
  3. Track — Record token usage, latency, and cost via the interception layer
  4. Score — Evaluate each output using eval_fn(expected, actual)
  5. Aggregate — Compute mean accuracy, latency, and estimated cost
  6. Rank — By default, sort by accuracy (ties broken by latency, then price). If you pass optional lambda_cost / lambda_latency on the selector, rank by the scalar combined objective instead.

Different selection algorithms vary in how they choose which combinations to evaluate, but steps 1-6 are the same for all of them.

docs.title: Parallel Evaluation
docs.text:
select_best(parallel=True, max_concurrent=20) permits concurrent evaluations where the selected algorithm supports them. The limit controls concurrent agent evaluations; an agent can itself issue several LLM calls within one evaluation.

Selector Parallel behavior Gittins One configuration per adaptive visit, with at most min(batch_size, max_concurrent) questions in flight. Warm-start questions are sequential for dollar accounting. Random configurations One configuration at a time; questions run in chunks of at most max_concurrent when parallel=True. Random questions Sequential shared-question sweeps over all configurations. UCB max_concurrent controls both acquisition batch size and evaluation concurrency. The parallel flag is ignored. Bayesian optimization Splits slots between configurations in an acquisition batch and the questions for each configuration. 
results = selector.select_best(parallel=True, max_concurrent=4)

Gittins' statistical batch size is configured on the constructor (batch_size), independently of the concurrency limit. For single-objective Gittins, the DP still models one question per transition. A final dataset tail can contain fewer questions than the configured batch size.

Gittins, UCB, and Bayesian optimization accept a soft dollar cap. Gittins checks estimated charges before adaptive batches, but actual charges can exceed the estimate. UCB checks spending between acquisition batches; Bayesian optimization checks between complete configurations or parallel acquisition batches. Already scheduled work finishes and can exceed the cap. Inspect selection_cost and search_cost_overshoot_usd. Smaller batches reduce the work between checks. Random baselines report costs without a dollar cap.

docs.title: Progress and cooperative stopping
docs.text:
on_update receives a result snapshot after completed work. Returning False, setting the supplied stop_event, or calling selector.request_stop() prevents a following batch from being scheduled. The currently scheduled batch finishes, including evaluations queued behind the concurrency limit; its results and charges belong to the final snapshot. Its is_final field is True and its reason is user_stopped.

For Gittins, the response time depends on the adaptive batch size, not just the concurrency limit: a batch can contain more questions than can run at once. Random configuration sampling checks for stopping between question chunks; random question sampling checks between configuration evaluations. UCB checks after an acquisition batch. Bayesian optimization completes the currently scheduled configuration or parallel acquisition batch. Smaller batches allow more frequent user decisions, while larger batches permit more concurrent work.

Use live selection for a callback and event example. Parallel execution does not change when a recommendation is eligible: incomplete random configurations or shared-question sweeps remain excluded even when some of their evaluations have finished.

docs.title: CrewAI
docs.text:
Using AgentOpt with CrewAI agents and tasks.

Model strings as llm parameter

CrewAI agents accept a model string via the llm parameter. Pass values from the models dict directly.

from crewai import Agent, Crew, Task
from agentopt import ModelSelector

class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.models = models

    def run(self, input_data):
        question = input_data if isinstance(input_data, str) else input_data["question"]

        planner = Agent(
            role="Planner",
            goal="Create a plan to answer the question",
            backstory="You are a planning assistant.",
            llm=self.models["planner"],
        )
        solver = Agent(
            role="Solver",
            goal="Answer the question following the plan",
            backstory="You are a problem solver.",
            llm=self.models["solver"],
        )

        plan_task = Task(description=f"Plan: {question}", agent=planner, expected_output="A plan")
        solve_task = Task(description=question, agent=solver, expected_output="An answer")

        crew = Crew(agents=[planner, solver], tasks=[plan_task, solve_task])
        result = crew.kickoff()
        return str(result)

selector = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent,
    models={
        "planner": ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini"],
        "solver":  ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini"],
    },
    eval_fn=eval_fn,
    dataset=dataset,
)

results = selector.select_best()
results.print_summary()

docs.title: LangChain
docs.text:
Using AgentOpt with LangChain's ChatOpenAI model instances.

Model objects, not strings

With LangChain, the models dict contains ChatOpenAI instances rather than plain strings.

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, SystemMessage
from agentopt import ModelSelector

class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.planner = models["planner"]  # ChatOpenAI instance
        self.solver = models["solver"]    # ChatOpenAI instance

    def run(self, input_data):
        question = input_data if isinstance(input_data, str) else input_data["question"]

        # Step 1: Plan
        plan = self.planner.invoke([
            SystemMessage(content="Create a brief plan to answer the question."),
            HumanMessage(content=question),
        ]).content

        # Step 2: Solve
        answer = self.solver.invoke([
            SystemMessage(content=f"Follow this plan and answer concisely:\n{plan}"),
            HumanMessage(content=question),
        ]).content
        return answer

def eval_fn(expected, actual):
    return 1.0 if expected.lower() in str(actual).lower() else 0.0

dataset = [
    ("What is the capital of France?", "Paris"),
    ("What is 2 + 2?", "4"),
]

selector = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent,
    models={
        "planner": [ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o"), ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")],
        "solver":  [ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o"), ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")],
    },
    eval_fn=eval_fn,
    dataset=dataset,
)

results = selector.select_best(parallel=True)
results.print_summary()

docs.title: OpenAI SDK
docs.text:
A two-step agent (planner + solver) using the OpenAI Python SDK directly.

Minimal setup

This is the simplest integration — just pass model name strings from the models dict to your OpenAI client calls.

from openai import OpenAI
from agentopt import ModelSelector

client = OpenAI()

class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.models = models

    def run(self, input_data):
        question = input_data if isinstance(input_data, str) else input_data["question"]

        # Step 1: Planner generates a plan
        plan = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=self.models["planner"],
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": "Create a brief plan to answer the question."},
                {"role": "user", "content": question},
            ],
        ).choices[0].message.content

        # Step 2: Solver executes the plan
        answer = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=self.models["solver"],
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": f"Follow this plan and answer concisely:\n{plan}"},
                {"role": "user", "content": question},
            ],
        ).choices[0].message.content
        return answer

def eval_fn(expected, actual):
    return 1.0 if expected.lower() in str(actual).lower() else 0.0

dataset = [
    ("What is the capital of France?", "Paris"),
    ("What is 2 + 2?", "4"),
    ("What color is the sky on a clear day?", "blue"),
    ("What is the largest planet in our solar system?", "Jupiter"),
    ("What is H2O commonly known as?", "water"),
]

selector = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent,
    models={
        "planner": ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],
        "solver":  ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],
    },
    eval_fn=eval_fn,
    dataset=dataset,
)

results = selector.select_best(parallel=True)
results.print_summary()

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Set up model selection for a multi-step agent using your own evaluation examples.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
AgentOpt evaluates candidate LLM combinations and recommends a configuration for your agent. Here's the idea:

  1. You define an agent class — it accepts a model config and runs on a datapoint
  2. You provide candidate models for each step of your agent
  3. AgentOpt tries different combinations, scores them, and reports the best ones
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  models = {                                                     │
│      "planner": ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],    │
│      "solver":  ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],    │
│  }                                                              │
│                                                                 │
│  For each combination (e.g. planner=gpt-4o-mini, solver=gpt-4o)│
│  AgentOpt does:                                                 │
│                                                                 │
│    agent = MyAgent({"planner": "gpt-4o-mini", "solver": "gpt-4o"})
│                                                                 │
│    for input_data, expected in dataset:                         │
│        output = agent.run(input_data)                           │
│        score  = eval_fn(expected, output)                       │
│                                                                 │
│  Then ranks all combinations by accuracy / cost / latency.      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Adaptive selectors decide which evaluations to run next based on the observations collected so far. Parallel evaluation can reduce waiting time, and response caching can reuse matching requests once a response is available. See Run Your Benchmark for live recommendations and stopping.

docs.title: Step 1: Define Your Agent
docs.text:
Write a class with two methods:

  • __init__(self, models) — receives a dict mapping step names to model names (e.g. {"planner": "gpt-4o-mini", "solver": "gpt-4o"})
  • run(self, input_data) — processes one datapoint and returns the output
from openai import OpenAI

class MyAgent:
    def __init__(self, models):
        self.client = OpenAI()
        self.planner_model = models["planner"]
        self.solver_model = models["solver"]

    def run(self, input_data):
        # Step 1: Plan
        plan = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model=self.planner_model,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Plan: {input_data}"}],
        ).choices[0].message.content

        # Step 2: Solve
        answer = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model=self.solver_model,
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": f"Follow this plan:\n{plan}"},
                {"role": "user", "content": input_data},
            ],
        ).choices[0].message.content
        return answer

No base class required

Just implement __init__ and run — duck typing only. Works with any framework: OpenAI, LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, etc.

docs.title: Step 2: Prepare Your Dataset
docs.text:
Create a list of (input, expected_output) tuples:

dataset = [
    ("What is the capital of France?", "Paris"),
    ("What is 2 + 2?", "4"),
    ("What color is the sky on a clear day?", "blue"),
    ("What is the largest planet in our solar system?", "Jupiter"),
    ("What is H2O commonly known as?", "water"),
    # ... ideally ~100 samples for reliable results
]

Dataset size

More samples means more reliable rankings. We recommend 50-100 samples for production decisions, but even 10-20 samples can surface clear winners during development.

docs.title: Step 3: Define Your Evaluation Function
docs.text:
Score agent output against the expected answer. Return a float in [0, 1]:

def eval_fn(expected, actual):
    return 1.0 if expected.lower() in str(actual).lower() else 0.0

The eval_fn is called on the output of agent.run(input_data) for each datapoint.

docs.title: Step 4: Run Model Selection
docs.text:
from agentopt import ModelSelector

selector = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent,
    models={
        "planner": ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],
        "solver":  ["gpt-4o", "gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],
    },
    eval_fn=eval_fn,
    dataset=dataset,
)

results = selector.select_best(parallel=True)
results.print_summary()

The models dict maps each step name (matching the keys your __init__ expects) to a list of candidates. AgentOpt picks one from each list, constructs MyAgent({"planner": pick1, "solver": pick2}), and evaluates it across your dataset.

With 3 candidates per step and 2 steps, that's 9 combinations. The default ModelSelector uses Gittins to allocate further evaluations after a warm start on each combination. Set observation_budget_fraction to limit configuration–question evaluations, optionally add max_search_cost_usd to limit spending, or stop while watching live recommendations. Single mode advises when to stop but continues by default; use stop_on_recommendation=True for automatic stopping. Use objective_mode="multi" to inspect accuracy/cost alternatives.

Optional: trade accuracy for cost or latency

Add lambda_cost=0.3 and/or lambda_latency=0.2 to the selector constructor to rank combinations by a scalar combined objective instead of accuracy alone. Omit them (default 0.0) for accuracy-first selection. Details: Combined objective.

docs.title: Step 5: Use the Results
docs.text:
# Get the winning combination
best = results.get_best_combo()
print(best)  # {"planner": "gpt-4o-mini", "solver": "gpt-4.1-nano"}

# Save the result, even if an early stop leaves no eligible recommendation
from pathlib import Path
Path("results.json").write_text(results.model_dump_json(indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
if best is not None:
    results.export_config("optimized_config.yaml")

docs.title: Reuse Cached Responses
docs.text:
In local mode, caching is enabled by default in .agentopt_cache. Choose a directory to keep responses for repeated runs of this benchmark:

from agentopt.proxy import LLMTracker

tracker = LLMTracker(cache_dir="./llm_cache")
selector = ModelSelector(
    ...,
    tracker=tracker,
)

Re-running after a stop

Create a new selector to start another run. Identical requests already saved in the cache can reuse responses without another provider call. New or changed requests can still incur charges, and scoring and selection still take time. Stopping does not save a resumable selection checkpoint; disk caching preserves responses, not the selector's progress. A forced process exit can lose entries not yet flushed to disk. See Response Caching.

Next steps:

  • Run Your Own Benchmark — Load examples, watch recommendations, stop a run, and choose nondefault settings
  • Selection Algorithms — Choose a smarter strategy for large model spaces

docs.title: Run your own benchmark
docs.text: AgentOpt evaluates your agent on examples you supply, shows the current model recommendation as evaluation progresses, and lets you stop with the observations collected so far. You provide an agent, candidate models, input/answer pairs, and a scoring function. There is no benchmark upload step: your Python program passes the dataset directly to ModelSelector.

docs.title: Prepare examples and a scorer
docs.text:
The Python API accepts a nonempty sequence of (input_data, expected_answer) pairs. For a text task, a JSONL file is a convenient way to store them:

{"input": "What is 2 + 2? Reply with only the answer.", "expected": "4"}
{"input": "What is the capital of France? Reply with only the answer.", "expected": "Paris"}

The terminal runner requires nonempty strings for both input and expected. Each line is one JSON object. Load the records and convert them to pairs before passing them to the selector; dataset does not accept a filename or a generator. For this format, the example runner below supplies a validated loader:

from examples.selection.benchmark_runner import load_dataset

dataset = load_dataset("my_benchmark.jsonl")

That import is for a repository checkout. In your own application, the basic conversion is:

import json
from pathlib import Path

records = [json.loads(line) for line in Path("my_benchmark.jsonl").read_text(
    encoding="utf-8"
).splitlines() if line.strip()]
dataset = [(record["input"], record["expected"]) for record in records]
if not dataset:
    raise ValueError("Provide at least one benchmark example")

def eval_fn(expected, actual):
    return float(str(expected).strip().casefold() == str(actual).strip().casefold())

eval_fn(expected, actual) is synchronous and returns a boolean or a finite numeric score; higher is better. This scorer uses exact matching after trimming whitespace and ignoring case. Replace it with a task-appropriate metric, such as answer extraction followed by numerical comparison. Gittins and random methods expect scores in [0, 1] by default; set score_bounds=(low, high) for a different range. The result field named accuracy contains your metric's mean, even if that metric is not classification accuracy.

Inputs and reference answers can also be dictionaries or other Python objects. Your agent's run(input_data) must accept the input, and your scorer must handle the expected answer and agent output. Convert CSV, Hugging Face, or other data sources into the same sequence of pairs. Use representative examples for model selection and a separate held-out set when reporting generalization performance.

docs.title: Try a complete terminal run
docs.text:
The repository includes benchmark_runner.py and a small illustrative dataset. From the repository root, install the checkout and the OpenAI SDK in a Python 3.12+ environment:

python -m pip install -e . openai

Set OPENAI_API_KEY in your environment. The following command makes real API calls; replace the model names with ones available to your account:

python examples/selection/benchmark_runner.py \
  --dataset examples/selection/benchmark_sample.jsonl \
  --models gpt-4o-mini gpt-4.1-nano \
  --output results.json

The runner uses one model node and the exact-match scorer above. Its sample data illustrates the file format and controls; it is not a benchmark for comparing model quality. Replace --dataset with your own JSONL file. For a multi-step agent, use the Python integration below and provide candidates for each node.

As work finishes, the terminal displays the evaluation count, search spending, and current recommendation. Press Ctrl+C to request a stop. The runner waits for scheduled work to finish and saves the final result to results.json, including when you stop before any recommendation is available. Keep the process running while it finishes that work; force-quitting bypasses this save step.

If authentication, rate limits, model calls, or scoring fail, the runner prints an English error and exits with a nonzero status. Correct the credentials, quota/concurrency, agent, or scorer before retrying. It does not print raw provider response bodies or reference answers in its error messages.

When a result snapshot is available, it is saved separately as results.partial.json (or <output-stem>.partial.json for your output path), leaving the complete output file untouched. The file includes is_partial, failure_message, and snapshot_scope. It contains the last available snapshot; failed or unfinished work and its charges may be missing. If no snapshot is available, or saving fails, the terminal explicitly says no results were saved. Partial results are for inspection, not a resumable checkpoint.

Useful variations, appended to the command above:

What you want Arguments Accuracy/cost alternatives --objective-mode multi Random shared questions, about 20% of the dataset --method random_questions --evaluation-fraction 0.2 Random complete configurations, about half of the candidates --method random_configurations --evaluation-fraction 0.5 UCB with an evaluation allowance --method ucb --evaluation-fraction 0.5 Gittins with a soft search-dollar limit --max-search-cost-usd 1.0 End automatically on single-objective Gittins advice --stop-on-recommendation

Small datasets can make a fraction too small to fund a warm start or even one complete random sampling unit. See the allowance rules below. Run python examples/selection/benchmark_runner.py --help for the runner's options; the Python API exposes further controls.

docs.title: Connect your agent and display live results
docs.text:
An agent is a class with __init__(self, models) and run(self, input_data); models contains the selected candidate for each node. No AgentOpt base class is required. The Quick Start defines a two-step MyAgent using this interface. With that class and the dataset/scorer above:

from pathlib import Path
from threading import Event
from agentopt import ModelSelector

stop = Event()
objective_mode = "single"  # use "multi" for accuracy/cost alternatives

selector = ModelSelector(
    agent=MyAgent,
    models={
        "planner": ["gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],
        "solver": ["gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4.1-nano"],
    },
    dataset=dataset,
    eval_fn=eval_fn,
    objective_mode=objective_mode,
)

def show_progress(snapshot):
    spend = snapshot.selection_cost
    spend_text = "unavailable" if spend is None else f"${spend:.6f}"
    print(f"Evaluations: {snapshot.total_evaluations}; search cost: {spend_text}")
    if objective_mode == "multi":
        candidates = snapshot.get_recommendations()
        if not candidates:
            print("Collecting observations; no recommendation yet.")
        for candidate in candidates:
            print(candidate.combo, candidate.conservative_accuracy,
                  candidate.conservative_cost_usd)
    else:
        print("Current recommendation:", snapshot.get_best_combo())
    if snapshot.stop_recommended and not snapshot.is_final:
        print("Gittins recommends stopping; you may stop now or continue evaluating.")
    if snapshot.is_final:
        print("Finished:", snapshot.stop_reason)

results = selector.select_best(
    parallel=True, max_concurrent=4,
    on_update=show_progress, stop_event=stop,
)
Path("results.json").write_text(results.model_dump_json(indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

To connect a Stop button, run selection in a worker thread and have the button call stop.set() or selector.request_stop(). The callback executes in the selection thread: send snapshots to your UI using that framework's thread-safe mechanism. selector.latest_results provides a copy of the latest snapshot for polling. A callback can also request a stop by returning False.

The package supplies progress callbacks and result objects. The terminal runner provides a ready-to-use display; a web dashboard or notebook interface needs to connect these callbacks to its own controls.

Updates happen after completed evaluations or batches, not while a model streams tokens. Gittins needs its uniform warm start before it can recommend a configuration. Random configurations require a completed configuration; random questions require a completed sweep across every configuration. Stopping earlier still returns observed records but can leave the recommendation empty. UCB recommends from observed configurations; Bayesian optimization recommends only fully evaluated configurations. See update boundaries for each method.

In single mode, get_best_combo() returns the current winner. Gittins bases that choice on a prediction for the complete supplied dataset; its model predictions are available through get_recommendations(). The raw results rows hold the observed scores. In multi mode, there is no unique best: use get_recommendations() to display the alternatives, then express a preference:

# For multi-objective results:
chosen = results.choose(max_cost_usd=0.01)  # deployment cost per question
if chosen is not None:
    print(chosen.combo)

These estimates describe the supplied benchmark. A live recommendation can change and is not a guarantee of future performance.

docs.title: Stop and keep the result
docs.text:
All supported methods allow a user stop. Stopping is cooperative: the currently scheduled batch finishes, including requests queued behind a concurrency limit; no next batch starts. It does not cancel or refund an in-flight model call. The final snapshot has is_final=True; a user stop is recorded as stop_reason="user_stopped".

Single-objective Gittins also publishes stop_recommended. By default, stop_on_recommendation=False, so this is advice and evaluation continues. Set stop_on_recommendation=True to finish automatically on that advice. The advice may change after further observations. Use is_final and stop_reason, rather than the advice flag, to tell whether the run has ended.

Saving results.model_dump_json() preserves the evaluation records and result fields for inspection. When single mode has a winner, you can also export its model configuration:

if results.get_best_combo() is not None:
    results.export_config("selected_models.yaml")

Stopping does not create a resumable checkpoint. There is no pause/resume API for restoring the selector's search state. A new run starts selection again. Disk caching, enabled locally at .agentopt_cache by default, can reuse saved responses for identical LLM requests. It does not restore the selection state or guarantee that every request in the new run is cached.

docs.title: Choose an algorithm and change defaults
docs.text:
The default is method="auto", objective_mode="single": Gittins recommends one configuration, with cost_scaling_factor=1e-4 for search cost and no deployment cost or latency penalty. A budget is optional. Without a user stop or an explicit limit, single-objective Gittins and both random methods can evaluate the full finite grid. Multi-objective Gittins also has an algorithmic termination rule.

method Single objective Multiple objectives auto, gittins Gittins winner Gittins accuracy/cost recommendation set random_configurations Random complete configurations Same sampling, empirical accuracy/cost alternatives random_questions Shared random questions across all configurations Same sampling, empirical accuracy/cost alternatives ucb UCB adaptive evaluations Unsupported bayesian Bayesian optimization of complete configurations Unsupported

random is a single-mode alias for random_configurations; matrix_ucb is an alias for ucb. Bayesian optimization requires python -m pip install "agentopt-py[bayesian]" (or python -m pip install -e '.[bayesian]' in a checkout). Gittins, random, and UCB are included in the standard installation.

docs.title: Set an evaluation allowance or dollar limit
docs.text:
Let K be the number of model configurations and N the number of examples. One cell is one evaluation of a configuration on a question; the full grid has K × N cells. For two nodes with two candidates each, K is four.

Method Fraction parameter and default Allowed dollar limit Gittins observation_budget_fraction=1.0 of K × N cells max_search_cost_usd=None by default Random configurations observation_budget_fraction=1.0, spent on whole N-question configurations None; actual spending is reported Random questions observation_budget_fraction=1.0, spent on whole K-configuration question sweeps None; actual spending is reported UCB observation_budget_fraction=1.0 of K × N cells max_search_cost_usd=None by default Bayesian optimization sample_fraction=0.25 of K configurations, at least two when available max_search_cost_usd=None by default

A 20% cell allowance does not generally mean 20% of distinct questions. For random_questions, it means approximately 20% of questions shared by every configuration; for random_configurations, approximately 20% of configurations, each evaluated on every question. Fractions round up to cells, and random methods only start whole units that fit, so some allowance may remain unused.

Gittins and random methods also accept max_total_question_evaluations, combined with the fractional cap. Gittins must have enough cells for its warm start: K × min(warm_start_batch_size, N). Random methods require enough cells for at least one whole configuration or shared-question sweep. A tiny dollar limit can stop Gittins during warm start, before any recommendation is available.

Dollar limits apply to new non-cached search charges and are soft: scheduled work can overshoot. Inspect selection_cost and search_cost_overshoot_usd. Random methods do not accept max_search_cost_usd. All methods can use user stopping with or without an evaluation allowance.

docs.title: Tune behavior beyond budgets
docs.text:
Pass selector parameters to ModelSelector(...); pass execution controls to select_best(...).

Control Default and effect models, dataset, eval_fn You supply the search space, examples, and quality metric. Gittins cost_scaling_factor 1e-4, single mode only. Scales raw USD search evaluation cost in its index/stopping calculation; it is not a dollar cap. lambda_cost, lambda_latency Both 0.0, single mode only. Penalize normalized deployment cost/latency in the final scalar objective. These are separate from cost_scaling_factor. Gittins stop_on_recommendation False. Set True for automatic stopping on single-objective advice. Gittins warm_start_batch_size, batch_size Both 4: initial questions per configuration, then questions per adaptive visit. A smaller adaptive batch gives more frequent updates and stop checks. select_best(parallel=False, max_concurrent=20) Execution defaults. The runner uses parallel evaluation with a limit of four. UCB uses max_concurrent for both its batch size and concurrency and ignores parallel. seed Gittins/random default 42; UCB defaults to None. Controls selection sampling, not model-provider randomness. Bayesian optimization has no selector seed argument. score_bounds Gittins/random default (0.0, 1.0). Must contain every score returned by the scorer. model_prices Optional mapping of model name to input_price and output_price, in USD per million tokens. Supply it for unknown models or price overrides. tracker Optional LLMTracker, for example with a cache_dir for disk caching.

Gittins and random selectors require tracked token usage and known nonnegative prices for every evaluated workflow. Changing the scorer or agent must preserve that tracking. The selector API reference also documents Gittins' prior/noise settings, recommendation conservatism, multi-objective search parameters, UCB exploration parameter a, and Bayesian batch_size.

docs.title: Contribute a benchmark example
docs.text:
To share an integration with other users, open a pull request to the AgentOpt repository with:

  1. A runnable example under examples/selection/, with the agent, data loading, and scoring code. Use local/ for a framework-specific local integration.
  2. A small redistributable sample or instructions to obtain the dataset, its source and license, and the split used for selection and final evaluation.
  3. A README entry giving the installation steps, credential environment-variable names, run command, candidate models, metric, and evaluation limits. Include how to see progress, stop, and inspect the saved result.
  4. Reproduction details for any reported results: dataset version, model IDs, selector parameters and seeds where supported, pricing assumptions, and whether cached responses were used.

Keep credentials out of the example and distinguish illustrative output from measured results. Test data loading and scoring on the small sample; any automated tests should be able to run without paid model calls. You do not need to contribute a pull request to run your own private benchmark.
